title: Slow rhythm, worsening perfusion
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: Mrs. Teresita Morales, 69, takes a beta-blocker and amlodipine, had diarrhea over the weekend, and arrives on Monday weak and dizzy in Cebu City. Heart rate 36, pressure 82/50, pale and slow to answer. You are the physician-on-duty. The potassium result will take 40 minutes.

n1.prompt: Is she stable, and what do you suspect?

choices.text: Unstable bradycardia; suspect hyperkalemia with the beta-blocker (BRASH).
choices.feedback: Stability is judged by signs; a slow rhythm in a dialysis patient on an AV-nodal drug is potassium until proven otherwise. Low pressure and slow responses make her unstable; dehydration is the likely trigger.

choices.text: Stable: the rate is slow but she is talking, so observe and repeat the vital signs in 15 minutes.
choices.feedback: Low pressure and slow responses are signs of compromise.
choices.then: Her pressure falls to 78/44; you treat her as unstable.

choices.text: Beta-blocker overdose only: hold the drug, give fluids and observe, since her potassium is usually controlled.
choices.feedback: The dose is usual; potassium and the drug together are the likely mechanism.

n2.prompt: What is your treatment plan now?

choices.text: Atropine per protocol, IV calcium, insulin with glucose, pacing or epinephrine if no response; call the attending.
choices.feedback: Treat the rate and the potassium together; atropine often works poorly in potassium- and drug-driven block. Atropine 1 mg without delaying the rest, per the order set; cautious saline; the attending decides on urgent dialysis.

choices.text: Atropine every 3 minutes until the rate rises, and nothing else yet, so you can see how she responds before adding drugs.
choices.feedback: Atropine alone may fail and delays potassium treatment; the maximum is 3 mg.
choices.then: After 3 mg with no change, you give calcium and insulin and prepare to pace.

choices.text: Adenosine to “reset” the rhythm, then repeat the ECG to see whether the pattern has changed before the next step.
choices.feedback: Adenosine slows AV conduction further and is for regular narrow tachycardia.
choices.then: The nurse questions the order; you switch to atropine, calcium and insulin.

n3.scene: The potassium returns at 6.9 mmol/L. Her rate is 46, pressure 90/56, more alert.

choices.text: Connect her now for urgent, monitored dialysis on the attending’s plan.
choices.feedback: Dialysis is the definitive treatment; calcium and insulin only buy time. The physician orders the potassium bath; check glucose after the insulin.

choices.text: Delay dialysis until tomorrow since she is better, and repeat the potassium in the morning before deciding.
choices.feedback: Shifting treatments wear off and potassium rebounds.

end.title: 9:30 a.m.
end.text: After dialysis her rate is 70 and her pressure 118/68. The attending reviews her beta-blocker and the reason she became dehydrated.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Stability by signs, not the number.
  • BRASH: potassium and an AV-nodal drug slow the heart together; treat both.
  • Dialysis is the cure for potassium-driven bradycardia; connect with the attending’s plan.
